subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON APPOINTMENTS, ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON APPOINTMENTS, ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to move concurrence of the house in the report of the select special committee on civil service matters, I desire at the very outset to express my personal gratitude to the members of the committee for the effort which each of them made to present every aspect of the situation without evidence of partisanship. In the deliberations of the committee subsequent to its open sittings they demonstrated a very high sense of public duty.
Although the report presented to the house is unanimous, it is not to be expected that men from different vocations in life who have been subject to different environment should reach those conclusions by the same processes of reasoning, and hence I wish to make it clear that in what I have to say in moving concurrence of the report I am expressing my own views which led me to those conclusions.
Civil service legislation was first introduced in Canada in 1868. That legislation set up a civil service board consisting of fourteen deputy heads of departments, five of whom should be a quorum to exercise all the functions of the board. A chairman and a secretary were to be chosen annually from among the fourteen. The duties of the board were, inter alia:	,
(a) To examine candidates; (b) keep a record of the candidates for examination; (c) grant certificates of qualification to candidates whose fitness and capacity, and whose testimonials as to moral character have been found satisfactory; (d) to investigate and report upon claims for promotion; and (e) to perform such duties as the governor in council thought fit; and to investigate such matters as might be referred to them connected with the administration of the civil service as to promotion, appointment, salary or the efficiency and welfare of the service; and to summon and examine witnesses and to call for persons and obtain papers.
From the resume of the legislation it is apparent that the boaird had to some extent the functions of bath our present civil service commission and a parliamentary committee. Some amendments to that legislation were made in 1872. In 1882 the two previous enactments were repealed arid the Canada Civil Service Act of that year was enacted. This legislation provided for a board of examiners of three members-
-who from time to time shall be appointed by the governor in council, to examine all candidates for admission to the civil service of 41761-179
Canada, and to give certificates of qualification to such persons as are found qualified according to such regulations as shall be framed for the guidance of the board.
There were two examinations prescribed: (a) a preliminary examination to decide if the applicant could read, write and add; (b) a qualifying examination to decide his fitness to fulfil any position for which he might be a candidate. The board had first to satisfy itself as to the man's age, health and character. The examinations were open to all and might be held in either language. By chapter 46 of the statutes of 1885 a consolidation of the acts of 1882, 1883 and 1884 was made, and the board of examiners was placed under the supervision of the Secretary of State. Provision was made for a secretary and a clerk to assist the board.
No change of any moment was made in the legislation I have just outlined until the Civil Service Amendment Act of 1908, which for the first time provided for a civil service commission consisting of two members appointed by the governor in council. Each commissioner was to hold office during good behaviour and could be removed by the Governor General on address of the Senate and House of Commons. The then existing civil service examiners were to continue during pleasure, but under direction of the commission.
It will be observed that up to this legislation of 1908 we 'had in Canada in respect of civil service matters a merit system, namely, a system by which only those holding the certificate of qualification from the examiner could be appointed to a position in the civil service. By this act of 1908 there was introduced what is now commonly called the merit system, but which in reality is something more; that is, this act with its amendments established a competitive merit system, whereby the person ranking highest in qualifications shall at all times be appointed to the vacancy which is to be filled. By this act appointment was to be made as a result of competitive examinations, and promotion was to be made for merit :by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the department, based upon the report in writing of the deputy head, accompanied by a certificate of qualification by the commission, to be given with or without examination as determined by the regulations of the commission.
By the amending act of 1918 the commission was to consist of not more than three members, and the tenure of office of future commissioners was to be for ten years during good behaviour. It also provided for the

retirement of a commissioner at the age of sixty-five. That act, subject to some minor amendments, is the Civil Service Act of today which is found in the revised statutes of 1927, and in respect of which a reference was made to your committee.
It might be well at this time to outline the nature of the organization of the Civil Service Commission. It can be divided into four main classifications, namely the examination branch, the organization branch, the assignment branch and the administration branch, and the last branch in turn may be subdivided into three, namely the secretarial, the personal services and the central register. Under the control of the Civil Service Commission there are approximately 35,000 civil servants. There are in Canada a total of 45,581 civil servants, as of March, 1931. Briefly, these are divided as follows: Permanent employees at Ottawa, 8.009; permanent employees outside Ottawa, 24,706, or a total number of permanent em-employees of 32,715. There are in Ottawa temporary employees numbering 3,757, and outside of Ottawa 9,109, or a total of 12,866 temporary employees. If you add together those two subtotals you get a grand total of 45,581 employees for the month of March, 1931, who that month received in salaries the sum of 15,905,303.97. In those figures there are not included the non-enumerated classes of employees, rural postmasters, casual labour, fee office positions and so on, who received in March, 1931, in compensation for their services, a further sum of 81,990,287.51, making a total payment by this government for the civil service, for the month of March, 1931, of $7,895,591.48.
For the purpose of determining who shall be appointed to the civil service of Canada there is prescribed an examination system, and in their nature these examinations are threefold. They may be written, they may be oral, they may be a rating for education and experience, or any combination of any two or three of the methods I have outlined. Oral examinations are held throughout Canada by a local representative of the Civil Service Commission, in conjunction with one or more representatives of the department, and now usually a representative of the Canadian Legion. Rating boards consist of a representative of the commission and one representative or more of the department. According to the theory of the examination system, these rating boards should always have upon them a representative of the commission, and it must be borne in mind that these boards make their ratings on a man's education and experience from an application form which has been submitted by him, in respect of 
which there has been little if any check as to the accuracy of the statements therein contained, and these ratings are made without the boards seeing the candidates who are applying for the positions in question.
I said the theory was that there should be on each rating board a representative of the commission, but from the data and material filed with the committee it appeared, in selecting at random some of the rating boards for different years, that on many such boards there was no representative of the commission. For example, in the Department of Agriculture in 1925 there were fifty-five competitions, but there were representatives of the commission on only twenty-six of those boards, while in connection with the fifty-five competitions there were eighty-one departmental representatives on the boards. In the Department of External Affairs during the years 1925, 1926, 1928 and 1930 there were four competitions. On only one of those boards was there a representative of the commission, while on the four boards there were six representatives of the department. In the Insurance department, in the years from 1925 to 1931, there were seven boards, on not one of which was there any examiner other than those appointed to represent the department.
Then there is brought into this examination system what are known as weights. It will be apparent that where the appointment to a position is determined by a percentage based on the combination of an oral examination and the rating given by a rating board, if a man is rated sufficiently high by the board and that rating is given sufficient weight as against the oral examination, while he may have qualified highest in the oral examination he may not get the position as a result of the recommendation of this rating board. For example, in the case of one appointment, of which we had the details before the committee., an appointment was to be made to a position by an oral examination and by a rating for education and experience. The weight given to the oral examination was only three, while the weight given to this rating for education and experience was seven.
May I point out to the house the effect of that weighting. As an illustration let me assume that candidate A is given 80 marks on his oral examination. If you multiply that by the weight of three you get a total of 240. Then let me assume that the rating board gives him a mark of only 60, and bear in mind that this rating board acts upon the application only, with no personal knowledge or observation of the man. If you multiply that mark by the weight of seven you get 420, and adding the two totals together gives

Civil Service-Report of Committee
a grand total of 660. Dividing that by 10 gives candidate A an average of 66 per cent.
Then take candidate B. On the oral examination he receives only 60 marks as against the man who received 80. You multiply that 60 by three and you get a total of 180. We will say that on the rating board he is given a rating of 80; multiply that by seven and you get a total of 560. If you add the 560 to the 180 you get a total of 740. In other words, he receives 74 per cent, but in the result the man who receives the highest mark on the oral examination is by no means declared the successful candidate, because by the operation of this weighting system, he may have a rating for education and experience which will not give him the highest percentage of qualification.
Time is not sufficient to permit me to outline to the house an instance which occurs in the evidence and which illustrates clearly the point I want to make. A. man gets a temporary appointment in a department on the recommendation of a departmental official: consider the fact that two of these departmental officials sit on the rating board as against one representative of the Civil Service Commission, together with the fact that a much higher weight may be given to the mark fixed by the rating board than the mark given by the oral examiners and you at once appreciate the opportunities there are in this system for what I will call, for want of a better word, abuses of the competitive merit system. In the case of written examinations there is little room for abuses. Before leaving the matter I wish to point out to the house the opportunities there are for creating those conditions of which we members of this House of Commons so frequently receive complaint. It is not possible for me, in the short time at my disposal, to deal with all the clauses of the committee's report; therefore I will confine the remainder of my remarks to three or four which, in my opinion, recommend the most marked changes in the present statute or regulations. But just in passing may I refer to one clause of the report which recommends an amendment, because on re-reading it, it occurred to me that it might not express with sufficient clearness the recommendation of the committee. Clause 9 of the report states;
Your committee recommends that section 60 of the Civil Service Act, as enacted by chapter 3S of the statutes 19-20 George Y, be repealed.
The intention of the committee was that the amendment which made possible the putting into the service of the private secretaries of ministers at a minimum salary of S3,120
41761-179J
per annum, should be repealed, but we do not suggest the repeal of that section as it stood prior to the 1929 amendment. The effect of the amendment w'hich the committee recommend will be that in future private secretaries of ministers will not be entitled to preference in appointments to the service, and can obtain admission thereto only through the usual channel of competitive examination.
I should like to refer to clause 18 of the report, in which your committee recommend that the secretary of the Civil Service Commission be called upon to perform only those duties which are peculiarly those of the secretary. The present secretary of the Civil Service Commission is one of the oldest employees in the civil service, in point of years of service, and during the years that he has been in his present position a practice has grown up of loading upon the secretary an enormous number of duties which are in no way related to the position. For example, all correspondence passes through his hands. Your committee can understand that it would be necessary for incoming correspondence to pass through the secretary's hands, but for the life of us we are unable to see why a query with respect to marks which some candidate made on examination should not be referred to the examination branch and replied to direct by the chief examiner. Again, recommendations of the organization branch with respect to matters of reorganization in departments or *with respect to classification pass through the secretary's hands, apparently for his approval or disapproval-matters which surely are entirely within the judgment of the Civil Service Commission. Therefore, in order to relieve this very worthy official of onerous duties which it is unnecessary for him to perform, we recommend to the commission the consideration of the change as suggested in the report.
Clause 20 of the report recommends that there be added to the committees of this house a select special committee on civil service matters. Time was not available to the members of your committee to introduce in evidence before the committee many files which some of us had read and from which it would appear that there were departmental abuses of the competitive merit system, as well as any which may have occurred in the administration of the civil service.
Temporary appointments are obtained on the requisition of a department in cases where, in my opinion, there was not in the beginning a bona fide intention that the employment should be temporary. By requisitions of departments and by statements made accompanying each of these requisitions, the Civil

Service Commission has been induced from time to time to extend and extend temporary certificates. At the moment I have in mind a case in one department where a young lady had been occupying the position of clerk, grade 3, for upwards of a year. Finally, when the commission insisted that there must be an open competition, the department said, "Very well, hold it." They held a competition, but the young lady who had been in that temporary position ranked second. So then, after much correspondence and delay, the department had this position reclassified and the young lady who had originally held one classified position for upwards of a year was immediately re-appointed temporarily to the new classification, though really doing the same work in the same department for the same pay and under exactly the same conditions.
Your committee did not have time to deal with many of these phases of the matter, but we believe that if there were each year a select special committee of this house sitting in review upon matters such as I have outlined, we should then have taken a great step in curtailing any abuses which may exist in the present competitive merit system.
I come next to clause 25, in which your committee recommend that the orders in council therein specified be amended so as to exempt from the operation of the Civil Service Act the appointment of postmasters in revenue post offices where the revenue does not exceed $3,000 per annum. I know of no better way in which I can illustrate to this house things which have occurred with respect to the appointment of postmasters than to cite three of the many illustrations which hon. members may find in this evidence, if they care to peruse it. In 1926, for example, there was a vacancy for a postmaster at St. Arsene in the constituency of Temiscouata, province of Quebec. Under the system then in existence-it has since been changed slightly-the district superintendent or inspector of the Post Office Department was temporarily absorbed as an official of the Civil Service Commission. This poor, unfortunate man who may be totally unfamiliar with any particular locality or the residents thereof is called upon to go out and interview a number of persons who may be applicants for a position, then to come back and make a recommendation not to the Civil Service Commission, bear in mind, although he is their official, but to the Post Office Department, as to how he rates those individuals in order of merit, from a post office standpoint.
Recently the system has been slightly changed. In the old days he used to say,

"I rate them as follows: John Jones, Bill Smith and William Brown." Now they have imposed upon the poor man a much more onerous duty in which he must rate them by marks. He is called upon to go out and interview six, eight or ten men he has never seen before; he may have to conduct his interviews in the space of two hours, and must give marks. Hon. members may observe that the marks are 90, 87, 85, 83 and so on all down the line.
The inspector had to make a report with respect to the appointment of St. Arsene, and he did so. When he made his report he recommended as first in order of merit Mrs. Roy, the widow of the former postmaster, secondly Mr. Laforest and thirdly Mr. Rioux. He also pointed out that in the case of Mr. Laforest's appointment there would be a decrease in the cost of postal service to the government of $91.42 per annum, but that in the event of Mr. Rioux' appointment there would be an increase in the cost amounting to $60.95 per annum, a difference of approximately $150. The post office inspector further reported that the location offered by the second man in order of merit, Mr. Laforest, was a more central and a better location than that offered by Mr. Rioux. Mrs. Roy-or probably the better French pronunciation would be "Roi"-was disqualified for good and sufficient reasons, as appeared from the evidence. However instead of Mr. Laforest, who was rated second in order of merit, getting the appointment, the appointment of Rioux was made by Commissioners Tremblay and MacTavish by a majority decision from which the chairman of the commission dissented.
I think it might be well if I read to the house the decision of the chairman of the commission in dealing with that particular case. He said:
As Laforest has been placed second in order of merit and his site reported more central than Rioux/ the former costing the department less at present and the latter costing more, his education and experience being, to say the least, equally good with Rioux, I am in favour of Laforest's appointment.
Naturally your committee sought if possible to find a reason for this appointment. I do not know whether or not we have succeeded, but from a letter on the file I found that the then Postmaster General, long before the Civil Service Commission had received the report of the post office inspector upon which their judgment should be based, in writing to the Civil Service Commission said:
As the other two applicants appear to have equal ratings, may I suggest that E. Rioux would seem to meet the wishes of the people there, according to recommendations received.

Civil Service-Re-port of Committee
Then we find on the file another letter written by a reverend gentleman apparently to the Postmaster General, but finding its way to the files of the Civil Service Commission. In it is the following paragraph:
With my excellent friend, Mr. Jean Francois Pouliot, member of parliament for this county,
I have recommended to yourself and to Mr. J. F.mile Tremblay, a member of the Civil Service Commission, the immediate nomination of Mr. Ed. Rioux as acting postmaster.
In endeavouring to justify his judgment in that case before your committee Commissioner MacTavish told us he favoured the appointment of the second man over the first in order of merit because of the age of Mr. Laforest. However if hon. members would turn to the file of the Civil Service Commission with respect to the appointment of a postmaster at Belwood they would find that in that case Commissioners MacTavish and Tremblay appointed a man 71 years of age, although Laforest's age was only 60 years.
I must hasten on, and shall not take time to deal with the details of those appointments. Commissioner MacTavish attempted to justify that appointment on the ground that there had been a petition on the file in favour of Mr. White at Belwood signed by patrons of the post office. On examination of that petition we found it was signed by 19 persons. Then if hon. members would turn in the evidence to a record of the appointment of a postmaster at East Broughton Station they would find that Commissioners MacTavish and Tremblay recommended in that case the appointment of a man, whereas the other one whom Dr. Roche favoured had a petition filed in his favour signed by 500 patrons of that particular post office.
In view of comments which have been made with respect to this recommendation I think it would be well for me to read the dissenting judgment of the gentleman who was chairman of the commission. He says:
It does not require varied experience for the postmastership of East Broughton Station.
The reference there was to the fact that the man Dr. Roche favoured had had three years' experience. He continues:
Post office experience has always been emphasized by the department as entitling an applicant to preferential consideration. This is one of a number of instances where the order of merit appears difficult to explain except by the fact that the M.P. for the constituency has recommended the applicant who has been placed first. Mr. Vachon who has been assistant postmaster of this office for the last three years and who apparently is "persona grata" with the patrons of the office as evidenced by the petition of 500 in his favour, is in my opinion, entitled to the position.
If hon. members would like further illustrations the record of evidence filed with the committee's report is replete with them.
The next thing I should like to call to the attention of the house in connection with the appointment of postmasters is the recommendation of officials of the Post Office Department to your committee. We had the advantage of having before us Mr. Coolican, Assistant Deputy Postmaster General, and E. J. Underwood, superintendent of post offices for Canada. I cannot take time to read to the house in detail excerpts from the evidence, but if I may paraphrase and at the same time attempt to make a synopsis of it, it is as follows:
Revenue postmasters are not properly described as civil servants. A revenue postmaster has no superannuation, and does not necessarily do the work for which he is paid. Be gets an assistant to do it, and he is not paid from parliamentary appropriations. I do not think it was ever intended that revenue postmasters should be under the civil service.
. . . The above principle was recognized by past civil service commissions in that they recommended that revenue postmasters in offices with a revenue of less than $400 be exempt. ... I say the postmaster up to that point ($3,000 or $3,500) should be removed from the Civil Service Commission. In the matter of appointments they are civil servants, in all other respects they are not. It is impracticable to appoint all these postmasters by present methods.
I still read from the views of those officials:
It is not economical to appoint revenue postmasters under the present system and it involves a large expenditure of money.
Then there came before your committee representatives of the Canadian Postmasters' Association of Canada.

If I may have the unanimous consent of the house, I shall endeavour to be very brief, because I have only one or two other matters to which I desire to refer. The representatives of the Canadian Postmasters' Association came before your committee. Of course, let me make it quite clear that they were not asking that revenue postmasters be taken, so far as appointment is
2846	COMMONS
Civil Service-Report oj Committee
concerned, from under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission, but they pointed out to us that their status had been ill defined; that their position was an anomalous one, and in an attempt to rectify it, they asked us to make them full-fledged civil servants where they were appointees to revenue offices in excess of $3,000. For the reasons I have above outlined, your committee recommended that the appointment of postmasters to revenue offices, having a revenue of less than $3,000, be made by the Postmaster General. Some will say that this is a return to patronage. I say: Better far a retum to patronage, if that be patronage, than a continuation of rank hyprocrisy in respect to the way in which these postmasters have been appointed. One section of the press says that if this house approves this clause of the report, it will mean entering the thin edge of the wedge which will ultimately open wide the flood-gates for the tide of political patronage. I say that in my opinion if you adopt this clause of the report, you are plucking from the thigh of the merit system an infected thorn, which infection has already to some extent undermined public confidence in this country and which ultimately, if not removed, will destroy the merit system.
I should like to quote just for a moment from a book written by Robert Moses who, I think, is recognized as an authority on the British civil service. In 1914 he published a book entitled the history of the civil service of Great Britain. I read just one short paragraph because I think it is most applicable to the subject under discussion:
No one in England dreams of reverting to patronage now. Competition is the general rule; but time has shown that open competition is not feasible in some departments, for example, for lower situations where merely physical qualifications are necessary or for higher positions where proved technical skill or business experience are requisites.
In that statement I heartily concur.

that question. I thought I had taken some pains to point out, briefly, it is true, that postmasters were in no sense civil servants, nor have they had any of the benefits of the

speechtext:
Rural postmasters have
had no benefits whatever under the Civil Service Act except the doubtful benefit of appointment by the commission. It is true that section 29 of the Civil Service Act provides a preference for returned soldiers, but if the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) will read the order in council passed in 1922, P.C. 1053, and the amending order in council passed in 1929, P.C. 1751, he will find that they make provision for the preservation of the returned soldier preference, and the change in these orders in council as recommended by the committee would in no way interfere with the returned soldier preference.
With the permission of the house I should like for a few moments to deal with section 26 of the report wherein your committee recommended the retirement of the present commission. The Hon. Doctor Roche, chairman of the commission, is an honourable gentleman who has long served the public of this country as their representative in the House of Commons. Subsequently thereto he has given, so far as your committee have been able to observe, faithful, efficient and diligent service for fifteen years as a civil service commissioner of Canada. He has brought to that position a high sense of responsibility; but whether we like it or not, increasing years are bound to bring about a degree of physical disability which gradually saps one of that dynamic force and mental alertness which are necessary to guide the destiny of this great machine of civil service which has something over 45,000 employees. Because of the age which that honourable gentleman has reached, because of the fact that the statute now provides that all appointees to the commission, other than himself because his appointment preceded the

Civil Service-Report oj Committee
statute, be retired at the age of sixty-five years, your committee made a recommendation for his retirement. Coupled with that is a recommendation that there should be given to him as an expression of appreciation of the service he has rendered to this country an honorarium or gratuity.
With respect to the other two commissioners, the three instances I have brought to the attention of this house I think will justify this house in coming to the conclusion that neither of those two gentlemen possesses the qualities of judicial determination which are necessary for the high office of a civil service commissioner. Suffice it to say that because of the evidence adduced before us, because of opportunity we had of observing the character and demeanour of these two gentlemen, we deemed it advisable in the interests of the reorganization of this commission that they too should be retired. One of these gentlemen, Commissioner Tremblay, served faithfully and well for a number of years in the civil service of Canada prior to his appointment as commissioner. Both may be able, probably are able, in some other field of activity, and both have family responsibilities. In view of the facts that I have just outlined we recommend that with their dismissal there be paid to each of these gentlemen a gratuity.
It was not to be hoped, even though the report of the committee was unanimous, that it might meet with the unanimous approval of this house. We have endeavoured as a committee conscientiously to perform the duty and task which the house assigned to us and in the hope that our recommendations may meet with the approval of a substantial majority in this house I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Plunkett), that the second report of the special committee on the civil service and the Civil Service Act be concurred in.

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON APPOINTMENTS, ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I have but few remarks to make in connection with this report, but I feel that I owe it to myself and to my adherence to the Civil Service Act for many years to make them.
Taken as a whole it is my belief that this report has not strengthened the Civil Service Act nor has it added support to the merit principle, but on the contrary has in a large measure weakened both. It has not, for example, recommended the inclusion under the operation of the act of those branches of departments that are now excluded, such as the income tax branch, customs appraisers, and so on, and to that extent it is in my opinion a weak report.
Many of the recommendations are worthy ones, but most of them deal with mere technical or routine procedure. The principal changes recommended are, of course, the retirement of the civil service commissioners and the adjustments with regard to postmasters. With respect to the first I have nothing but the strongest approval of the recommendation of the committee. I have long felt from information at my disposal that action of this kind should have been taken, and I am in hearty agreement with the recommendation in that respect. I do wish, however, that the report had embodied the recommendation to replace the three-men commission with a one-man commission. I seriously believe that in the operation of an act of this character, if one has a good, strong capable man who retains public confidence, it is more likely that the act will be administered with the least possible friction and the least danger of encroachment.
In the matter of the postmasters, however, I find myself in serious disagreement with the recommendation of the committee in the main. The chairman (Mr. Lawson), who has just concluded an eloquent and excellent speech based on his report, offered as an explanation for the action of the committee several reasons. He cited three cases of appointments to post office positions which were of a questionable character. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, rising to speak briefly in support of the motion for adoption of the report, I wish first to express my very great pleasure on having been chosen a member of this somewhat important committee. That pleasure became greater as the work of the committee proceeded and it became apparent that the members intended to treat the evidence from a strictly impartial and non-partisan viewpoint. I think the very cordial feeling which existed throughout all our proceedings and which resulted in the presentation of this unanimous report is to be attributed in very large measure to the tact, good judgment and diligence of the chairman of the committee.
Throughout the proceedings I was particularly impressed by the very high type of civil servants and the able representatives of the various civil service organizations and the war veterans' association who appeared before the committee. The lucid and logical manner in which they presented their evidence created a most favourable impression.
My purpose this afternoon is to deal briefly with the major finding of the committee, that is, that the commissioners be retired. The retirement of those gentlemen will give the government of the day an opportunity to wipe the slate clean and start over again. The chairman has given to the house a full history of what led up to the Civil Service Act of 1918, which was subsequently amended by the act of 1927. It is with respect to the

Civil Service-Report of Committee
period from 1918 down to the present time that I propose to address my remarks. It is quite true that perhaps the findings of the committee as a whole do not meet with approval of everyone. That was to be expected. Nevertheless I think it speaks well for the manner in which the committee approached their work that, although composed of four Conservatives, two Liberals and a Labour member, they were unanimous in coming to the conclusion that the heads of the Civil Service Commission should be retired. Up to the time of the Civil Service Act of 1918 we did have a period when political patronage governed appointments to the civil service, and from that year down to the present time it may be said that we have been going through a transition period. The chairman has pointed out the immense power of those having, wholly or partially, jurisdiction over some 45,000 civil servants drawing in salaries every month in the neighbourhood of $7,895,000. I find that in 1919 when the present Civil Service Commission was appointed the salaries of the commissioners were fixed at $7,000 for the chairman, and $6,000 each for his two associates. It does seem to me that then and there a mistake was made, and that that mistake has not been rectified down to the present time. I contend that the salaries paid at that time were entirely inadequate to get the type of men needed to administer the affairs of this commission, which as I have said, has partial [DOT] or total control over the whole civil service. At that time it must be borne in mind, too, that the more important positions on the staff were filled at very low salaries. We find the chief examiner with an initial salary of $2,050, that the initial salaries of other examiners were from $1,800 to $1,850, and that the salaries for investigators in the organization branch were as low as $1,320. These were the salaries of the staff of a commission having jurisdiction over the civil service wherein the salaries of deputy ministers ran from $9,000 up to $12,000 a year, and in one case as high as $15,000, and the salaries in the higher branches of the various government departments ranged from $4,000 up to $6,000 a year. Yet at the inception of the commission it was attempted to appoint men at the salaries to which I have referred-men who were to have authority over the civil service. Bearing in mind that this commission and its staff have charge of appointments, promotions, classifications, organizations and reorganizations throughout the whole of the civil service, one would at least expect that the qualifications of the heads of that commission, and those occupying the higher positions in the staff, would be at least as great
as if not greater than those required of the people over whom they exercise control. This is one of the reasons to which I attribute the fact that, to some measure at least, the merit system was not given full force and effect from 1918 or 1919 to the present time. I am quite willing to admit that while many of these positions were filled at low salaries, with the experience subsequently gained they have given many valuable men to the commission, but these men have been educated and developed to fill the positions they now occupy, to some extent at least, at the expense of the public service.
Now we come to 1926, when two of the commissioners, Mr. Jameson and Mr. . Larochelle, were retired for reasons which are familiar to every hon. member. Later two new commissioners were appointed, Mr. Tremblay and Mr. MacTavish. Shortly after the appointment of these gentlemen an investigation was held into the staff of the commission by two subordinate officials of the commission itself, and from that investigation resulted what was known as the Kemmis and Simmons report. In connection with that investigation I want to point out that Mr. MacTavish and Mr. Tremblay, the two new commissioners appointed, had so little experience that they determined that the proper way to have an investigation into their own staff was not to have it undertaken by the heads of the departments but by two subordinate members of the staff, and the very fact that this investigation was held at that time indicated to me that from the very beginning these gentlemen were not the type or calibre of men that should have been appointed to the positions of junior commissioners. We had many instances brought before us where the commissioners differed, and where there were adverse findings. Then we come down to about a year or so ago, when we had the Bouchard trial and disclosures, and coming to the investigations of this committee, we have now recommended the retirement of these gentlemen.
In that connection I do not wish to do more than quote from an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen under date of April 9, 1932. Speaking of the commission, the editorial states:
The machinery is devised to give Canada air efficient, civil service free from patronage interference. The present weakness is in the controlling hands on the machinery.
The chairman of the Civil Service Commission, Hon. W. J. Roche, is generally trusted throughout the country. As a cabinet minister in Sir Robert Borden's administration, he had the respect of members on both sides of parliament.
2S50	COMMONS
Civil Service-Report oj Committee
I should say that this respect has continued throughout his entire eareer. I think ail hon. members will agree that Doctor Roche is a gentleman of the highest character. The editorial proceeds:
It is absurd, however, to pretend that the other commissioners, Messrs. Newton Mac-Tavish and J. E. Tremblay, have any such standing in public esteem or any such claim to the confidence of the country in the administration of the merit system. They were appointed without any record of service in public life or of outstanding administrative experience.
It is hardly surprising that members of parliament, cabinet ministers and deputy ministers are dissatisfied with such an exercise of authority by ^ commissioners of very limited experience. Until this weakness at the head is corrected, general dissatisfaction will very likely tend to grow in volume.
With those sentiments I am in entire accord. In another editorial appearing in the Ottawa Citizen of April 15, 1932, we have the following remarks with regard to the Civil Service Commission:
ri The merit system is evidently being abused. I he obvious weakness is in the absence of merit in some of the very positions where it is most needed, namely, on the board responsible for the administration of the Civil Service Act.
No matter how the law may be amended, it is liable to fail in the hands of incompetent commissioners. The present act has, on the whole, stood up well under a severe test for twelve years or more. It has been commended by authorities on civil service administration in other countries as one of the most advanced.
Hon. members of the house will note that while we have made a number of recommendations they are really minor in character and do not affect the merit principle or the main features of the act itself.
Undoubtedly it meant a real step forward for the merit system in Canada. Where it has appeared to fall short has been invariably due to faulty administration.
It is hardly surprising to find members of parliament restless when they know of undoubted instances of patronage of another form, even more demoralizing than political patronage, in the civil service. When members exercise patronage, at least they have to take the responsibility for it in the eyes of constituents. They can be held accountable in the next election.
When patronage is allowed by the Civil Service Commission, under an outside influence, fraud is being perpetrated on the public. The people of Canada are led to believe that positions are filled entirely on merit after an impartial examination of applicants, when it is notorious that methods of evading the law are countenanced.
Further on the editorial states:
It may be found that the Civil Service Act can be improved by some minor amendments, but improvement is most needed in the administration of the act. There has been a marked [Mr. Bowman.l
decline in public confidence in the Civil Service Commission, particularly in recent years. The remedy is to appoint commissioners whose standing in the country is calculated to restore public confidence as well as to gain the confidence of the civil service.
Again I say I am in complete accord with the views expressed in that editorial.
It must be borne in mind by all hon. members of the house that if the Civil Service Commission and its staff are to accomplish the work for which the commission was set up, there must be mutual respect and confidence as between the commission and its staff and the various departments of the public service. That mutual respect and confidence can be obtained only when the commissioners are men of high character, undoubted integrity and some administrative and executive ability. It does seem to me that during this transition period, if there has been any fault to be found with the commission and its work it has been due to weakness at the head and, because of that, perhaps weakness through the staff.
My principal object in saying anything at all at this time is to impress this view upon the government and respectfully to suggest that in appointing commissioners to take the places of those being retired they bear in mind the great importance of this commission and its staff, and see to it that men of character, of integrity and of the highest possible administrative and executive ability are appointed to these positions.
Consider these facts: that two years ago there was appointed a grain commission in western Canada, the chairman of which was paid a salary of 812,000; that two junior commissioners were paid 110,000 each; that each of the commissioners in the four western provinces receives either $7,000 or $7,500, I forget which; and that in Ontario there was paid to the chairman of the Liquor Control Commission a salary of $20,000 per annum, which I understand is to be reduced now to $10,000 to the present chairman, and then consider that we have been expecting during the last ten years to obtain from a commission receiving the salaries I have mentioned, of $7,000 and $6,000, men to control vastly more important offices and to discharge more important duties than either of these other commissions, though, of course, one must admit that the grain commission is of great importance.
I do not intend to say more than this in conclusion. I do respectfully submit to the government of the day, and I do so in confidence, knowing the great business ability of the present Prime Minister, that in the first

Civil Service-Report oj Committee
place the new commissioners should be given salaries commensurate with the positions they are to occupy, and secondly, that in the choice of commissioners men of outstanding character and integrity, men of marked administrative and executive ability should be sought. I submit that if this were done many of the troubles respecting the administration of the Civil Service Act and the civil service would eliminate themselves or be eliminated in a brief period of time.
During the proceedings of the committee evidence was given to the effect that often the procedure was quite circuitous and that there was a good deal of red tape. Well, that is all a matter of administration. With a strong man at the head of the commission and one or two capable junior commissioners, as the case might be, that would soon be overcome. It was established before the committee that there was much overlapping and overmanning in the service. Again, I am of the opinion that with a strong commission and an efficient staff that could be obviated. And may I point out that it would not necessarily result in throwing out of employment any number of the civil servants of Canada. I was surprised to learn that approximately ten per cent of the service retired annually from natural causes such as death, marriage, resignation, and so forth. The holding-up of appointments for a couple of years would mean that there would be nine or ten thousand vacancies to fill, which surely should afford considerable scope for cutting down any overlapping or overmanning that might exist. The same with respect to the amalgamation or merging of different sub-departments of the public service. With a strong commission and an efficient staff having the confidence of and working in close cooperation with the deputy heads of the service-for this is most important-there would soon be remedied any duplication of services such as we find at the present time. So in the matter of reorganization. The head of the organization branch stated that there had been no reclassification to any substantial extent in the service since 1921, that the work should be undertaken at the present time and in this connection the statement was made that with the staff he had it would take him about a year and a half or two years to do this work, which was now overdue. That practically concludes what I have to say.
I do not intend to refer particularly to the matter of postmasters but I would call attention to page 454 of the evidence where Mr. Coolican makes the following statement in answer to a question by myself:
Q. You think, Mr. Coolican, that that would lessen a lot of the difficulties?-A. Yes, I think it would, and the result would be just as good.
And at page 455, he makes this statement:
I think the same good results could be obtained in these cases over $400.
Similar remarks were made by Mr. Underwood at page 463. It must, of course, be borne in mind, indeed it must be perfectly clear to hon. members, that there was some give and take in order to enable us to arrive at a unanimous report. Perhaps the report itself is not perfect and does not meet with the approval of all hon. members; nevertheless I do say that in arriving at a unanimous decision to retire the present commissioners, and to submit to the house a recommendation that men of the right calibre and standing in the community be appointed to succeed them, the committee have accomplished at least some small measure of good.

I do not think there is a member of this hon. house who will doubt my sincerity in relation to the merit system in the civil service of Canada. If anybody wishes to compare my own draft with t'he report submitted in those days I do not think he will find very much difference between the two. Probably he has turned to the evidence with a view to justifying certain things done by the committee. Special reference was made by him to the St. Arsene case. I do not wish to go fully into the evidence, but if hon. members were at all interested they would find that the chairman of the commission decided one way, and that the two remaining commissioners, Messrs. Tremblay and Mac-Tavish, decided another way. Wide indeed as they were, I doubt very much the powers of the committee to investigate the use of discretionary powers, vested in these officials. If there is a ca^e wThere the commissioners had a right to exercise these discretionary and statutory powers, certainly it was in this case. I challenge anyone to say that in the exercise of these wide powers these two men did not exercise their powers in a way befitting their positions. Throughout the whole of the evidence it was revealed that whatever they did was amply justified. That is borne out in this case by a letter from Mr. Coolican, assistant deputy postmaster general, which I had placed on record, and which sums up the proceedings in the year 1927 as to who between Laforest and Rioux should have been appointed. The letter is to this effect:

That letter was filed simply to show that one man of a certain age rather than of another age had been appointed. Great stress was laid upon the fact, and the commissioners were blamed for appointing one man younger by some years than another. I hesitate to bring out these facts, because I thought it would not be necessary to do so. I do not like to refer to the Belwood post office, but I find it necessary to do so. It would have been much better for him to ignore it, but as the matter has been brought up I wish to refer to it. I regret very much to have to mention what happened in the committee, and I wonder if the chairman and the vicechairman of the committee got their inspiration from the hon. member for Long Lake (Mr. Cowan) when they were asking questions of the witnesses who appeared before them.
First a word as to the merit system. I wish to congratulate my good friend the senior member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) upon his very excellent speech. In fact, he is the one amongst us who knows most about the merit system, and he told his colleagues on the committee who did not know anything about the merit system, with the exception of my hon. friend from South Battleford (Mr. Val-lance), and a couple of others, what it was all about.
What happened about that case? It is very simple. Was there anything wrong about the 1926 appointment? No. Was there a report made? Yes. Who made it? Mr. S. Tanner Green, of Quebec, the man whom the former Postmaster General denounced in this house some time before his party took office. A man can do anything when he is asked to do that. That is the man who made the report. At whose instigation? At the request of Mr. Dube, the defeated Tory candidate in Temiscouata county-although I do not blame him for having done it. Now let me refer to page 126 of reference No. 110:
December 29, 1930.
In 1926, when tile old postmaster, Mr. J. W. Roy died, I recommended that the post office should be placed at Mr. Laforests place.
Mr. Green made a report which was sent to the Postmaster General. That report is dated September 14, 1926. Because the man put one name under the other the chairman of the committee thought it was a rating; in fact no rating was given. The date of this report, September 14, 1926, is the very day of the general election, and the inspection had been made in the preceding month of August while the shadow government was in power.

In fact the gentleman whom I have named before-I will not name him again lest I give him too much advertising-went to see Mr. Green and asked him to give a chance to that man. On the record is the letter which was sent to the Postmaster General this year. The report was made by Mr. Green in favour of that man at the request of the defeated Conservative candidate for Temiscouata county. There was no question of merit, both men were about equal. The only difference was that Rioux was much j'ounger. Mr. Laforest is nearer seventy than sixty and is too old to be appointed postmaster. The Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) wrote me that during the several years Rioux had been postmaster he had given good service, and he, the Postmaster General, had no objection to his application to the Civil Service Commission for the new appointment, if he provided a better place for the post office.
A great deal of fuss has been made over the recommendation by the parish priest on behalf of one of his parishioners. In the eyes of certain persons it was a great scandal. But the parish priest did not cause any harm to the other fellow. What happens in Catholic parishes is that when a suitable candidate goes to the parish priest for a recommendation he gets it, and the. recommendation simply means that the man is an honest and respectable citizen and fit for the job. We never see a parish priest fighting for one man as against another. In fact, his recommendation is just a certificate of good character, the same as is given probably by Protestant clergymen to the people who live in their community. As my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) quoted the Citizen, I desire to quote its contemporary, the Journal. In its issue of April 18 last appeared this very excellent editorial:
A Very Grave Matter
When Mr. J. Emile Tremblay, member of the Civil Service Commission, giving evidence on Thursday before the special committee of parliament investigating the Civil Service Act and its operation, told that he considered a certain candidate was "entitled" to the position of postmaster at St. Arsene "on the facts submitted to me, and on representations made to me by the parish priest to the effect that he was the choice of the whole population and his appointment was the most satisfactory," Mr. Tremblay was told by the vice-chairman of the parliamentary committee, Mr. J. L. Bowman, of Dauphin, Man., "this is a very grave matter, in my opinion." It would be interesting to know why.
The facts submitted were that the first name on the list reported on by the postal inspector was not acceptable by reason of difficulties experienced with that candidate in former association with that same office. The inspector

Civil Service-Report of Committee
had rated the candidate in his judgment "from a postal service point of view." The "second" and "third" candidates rated were about equal in education and experience, neither having had any post office experience.
But it was claimed by the inspector that the "second" candidate's accommodation for the post office would cost the postal department about $150 a year less than would that offered by the "third" choice.
In fact it was not proved to the committee that the mail carrier's pay was increased or decreased because he went here or there.
Commissioner Tremblay said the question of site was one for the post office to consider, not the Civil Service Commissioners, and he produced a ruling from the Department of Justice. He therefore "approved" the appointment of the "third" candidate on the ground of better personal qualifications.
It was when he mentioned that representations had been made to him by the priest of the parish in favour of the "third" candidate that the matter became "very grave" to one member of the committee apparently.
At the afternoon sitting of the committee that same day, Mr. Tremblay amplified his statement as to the representations made by the priest. He said:
"He told me his standing in the community was better than the other man. I think he said he had been mayor of the village, if I am not mistaken, and stood in better with the residents than the other man, and his appointment would be more acceptable to the patrons of the office. I am only speaking from recollection."	.
The appointment was six years ago, it should be stated.
What is there "grave" about all this? Dr. W. J. Roche, chairman of the Civil Service Commission, had told the committee that there had been "honest difference of opinion" among the three members of the commission, and that he had voted for the "second" candidate on the ground of saving to the postal department. He said he remembered nothing of any representations of the priest. When that same appointment came up for consideration again a year or so ago, all three commissioners voted for re-appointment of the man in dispute.
But the so-called "grave matter" turned into something of a comedy when Dr. Newton Mac-Tavish, the remaining member of the Civil Service Commission, took the witness stand. Dr. MaeTavish's evidence was that like Commissioner Tremblay, he considered the question of site was a concern of the post office, not of the Civil Service Commission, as the post office had the authority to refuse the appointee of the commission on that ground, if the officials liked.
And what was the determining factor in Dr. MacTavish's choice of the "third" candidate? Not representations of the priest. Doctor Mae-Tavish said he could not recall that any such considerations had come before him. The factor which weighed with him was simply that the "second" candidate was 62 years old, "and getting near the retirement age," while the "third" candidate, whose choice he approved, was 47 years old.
The fact that a "priest" had made representations to a member of the commission was discussed at some length by the parliamentary 41761-180
committee. Mr. Tremblay said he did not consider such representations were likely to be "political" and he took them into account in view of their nature. He had never seen the priest before then, he said.

Earl Lawson, remarked that members of parliament might be considered "reputable persons." Might not the same consideration be accorded to a "parish priest"? Roman Catholic or Protestant?

Last week we had a great hullabaloo over the fact that a priest, exercising his rights as a reputable citizen, recommended that a certain person be appointed as a rural postmaster. Why a clergyman, no matter of what faith, should not have the right to suggest that a certain person would make a competent public official, is beyond The Journal. S3,000,	the incumbents of those offices who now hold their positions by virtue of the Civil Service Act will be subject to summary dismissal, and new appointments may be made without any of the formalities prescribed by the Civil Service Act. I propose to take the strongest exception to that procedure.
I do not agree with what has been said with regard to the present position of these men. The chairman of the committee, when I questioned him, intimated that they were not under the Civil Service Act. I have respectfully to take exception to that statement. The senior hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) also suggested that they were not under the Civil Service Act. In order to refresh my memory I have looked at the act again and I want to put on record the provisions and the classifications therein and to submit to the house that those men are under the Civil Service Act in every sense of the word and entitled just as fully to whatever privileges and benefits are intended by the act to men in salaried positions. The difference is that they are not under the Civil Service Superannuation Act, which is a different act altogether. I want to make that clear because I presume the chairman of the committee, having made the statement he did, has some authority for it and will wish my reasons for differing from him. My reasons are these: in the Civil Service Act, which is chapter 22 of the revised statutes of Canada, section 2 (a) defines "civil service" as follows:
"Civil Service" means the civil positions and employees in and under the several departments of the government of Canada, and in the offices of the Auditor General, the Clerk of the Privy Council, the Governor General's Secretary, the Public Archives, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada, the Civil Service Commission, and all other civil positions under and persons in the civil employ of His Majesty, but not including the members of any commission or board appointed by the governor in council.
Paragraph (d) of section 2 defines "employee" as follows:
(Mr. Ralston.]
"Employee" means and includes officers, clerks, and employees in the civil service, but does not include deputy heads.
Let me point out to the house that the words "civil servants" never appear in that act; "civil servants" are not defined in it. "Civil servants" are defined in the Civil Service Superannuation Act for another purpose entirely. If hon. members read the Civil Service Act through, they will find the people referred to there are not referred to as civil servants, but the "service" is referred to and the people for whom positions are provided are referred to as "employees." Let me instance one or two sections. Section 13 reads:
The rate of compensation of an employee . . . shall beso and so. Section 14 also refers to the rate of compensation of an "employee," and in subsection 3 of this section the word "employee" is again used. Section 15 uses the term "temporary employee." When we look at the crux of the act which takes the jurisdiction away from the governor in council to make these appointments, it is not the term "civil servants" that is used, but in section 19 the words are:
Save as otherwise provided in this act or in any regulation made hereunder, neither the governor in council nor any minister, officer of the crown, board or commission, shall have power to appoint or promote any "employee" to a position in the civil service.
I submit on the face of the section itself, that ds so.

The words are that this classification and rates of compensation-
-are hereby ratified and confirmed, and the civil service shall, as far as practicable, be classified in accordance therewith.
I have under my hand a copy of the classification which was made in 1919 and confirmed by that act and although Mr. Underwood and Mr. Coolican say that parliament never intended that these rural postmasters should be under this act, I find on page 549 of the classification a provision for "Postmaster (grade 1 office)." They are not people quite outside the Civil Service Act to whom no consideration is to be given, as would be the case were Mr. Coolican and Mr. Underwood correct in their assumption regarding parliament's intention. Therefore there can be no question at all that these rural postmasters in post offices with revenue between $400 and $3,000 come under the Civil Service Act.
Then there is a provision that certain classes may be excluded from the Civil Service Act. It is in section 59 of the act as it stands today. Section 59 reads:
In any case where the commission decides that it is not practicable nor in the public interest to apply this act to any position or positions, the commission may-
Note this:
-the commission may with the approval of the governor in council, exclude such position or positions in whole or in part from the operation of the act, and make such regulations as are deemed advisable, prescribing how such position or positions are to be dealt with.
I submit that that is the only way the committee can accomplish the removal of these postmasters from the Civil Service Act; not by

saying they were not intended to be under the act but by admitting that they are at present under the act and by having the commission invoke the section I have just read and exclude them, but only if the circumstances are shown which the section mentions. Away back in 1922 an order in council, P.C. 1053, was passed in which the Civil Service Commission did recommend exempting from the Civil Service Act appointments to positions where the salary was not in excess of $200 per annum. Note this, that the commission itself recommended that provision and the governor in council approved it. Other positions were recommended to be exempted at the same time; for instance, positions for which the compensation provided consists of fees pertaining to the office, and positions of an honorary character' to which no compensation is attached; the position of orderly in the office of the governor general's secretary; the position of Indian interpreter, Department of Indian Affairs, which it can be readily understood was not a position that could be advantageously dealt with under the Civil Service Act; the position of physician performing the duties of port physician under the Department of Health at various ports, which are specified in a long list in the order in council; positions in the following classes of skilled and unskilled labour and domestic service, such as blacksmith; and that is followed by two pages of other positions ending with culler, running all the way from sawmill foreman to laundress, upholsterer, electrician foreman, sign painter, and so one. That order in council exempted all these special classes of employees from the provisions of the Civil Service Act.
May I say in passing that that exemption of positions up to $200 salary did not begin in 1922. It was contained in an order in council, P.C. 1694, passed in 1919, very soon after the Civil Service Act was passed. This was embodied in order in council 1053 of 1922, to which I have referred, and that continued to be the rule until in 1929 a slight amendment was passed and postmastei's in offices where the revenue did not exceed $400 were excluded. That was really the same office as the one to which the $200 salary applied because the postmasters had been getting fifty per cent of the revenue and two hundred dollars' salary represented fifty per cent of a revenue of $400. The postmaster's percentage was raised to 70 per cent and the order in council passed in 1929 simply changed the orovision so that the text was a $400 revenue

subtopic: REPORT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON APPOINTMENTS, ADMINISTRATION AND OPERATION OF CIVIL SERVICE ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before recess I had, I hope, convinced the house that rural postmasters in offices where the revenue is between $400 and $3,000 are members of the Civil Service of Canada and come under the Civil Sendee Act. I had made the distinction between employees of the civil service under the Civil Service Act and those who are designated by a different term, namely, civil servants, under the Civil Service Superannuation Act.
It may be asked, what advantage or benefit is there in being an appointee under the Civil Service Act, as these men are. I am not going into the matter in detail, but I would remind the committee that there are certain statutory provisions with regard to promotion contained in the Civil Service Act which apply to these men whom it is now proposed to-exclude from the benefit of that act. Provision for their compensation is made under the-Civil Service Act, and any increases in compensation are dealt with by the Civil Service-Commission. The duties which these men are performing, and the value of their services to the public, are all subject to appraisement by the machinery of the Civil Service Commission. Provision is made in the Civil Service Act for holidays-an express statutory provision of which these men also have the benefit. A very important provision is there, namely, that appointees to this service must be British subjects; that is contained in section 33. If these positions are taken out of the act these provisions do not apply. Further than that what are the provisions of the Civir Service Act, and what are the rules and regulations, which govern the tenure of office of these men who are in the service? As we know, the provision has not only been recognized by this house as stated long ago by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but it has been embodied in an order in council, and it has been restated' by the right hon. Prime Minister when on this side of the house and again since the present government took office, namely, that these postmasters hold their office and cannot be dismissed for partisanship unless there has-been a certificate by a member of parliament

Civil Service-Report oj Committee
that of his own knowledge they are guilty of partisanship, or there has been an investigation and an adverse decision given by the investigator. That is very important. That is the tenure under which these men hold office, and it has been acknowledged and recognized both by practice and by order in council. The proposal now is that these men shall be taken out of the Civil Service Act, that this practice and this order in council shall not apply, but simply by the action of the minister or the action of the governor in council, whether on recommendation or not-and from some things that have transpired in this house in the last week or two I do not know whether the government would even require a recommendation'-but in any case without a reason being given these men might be summarily dismissed from office without any charge, without any investigation, without any responsibility being taken by any one except by the minister concerned. I submit that that is not in the interests of the public service, and that men who are in those positions at this time-appointed thereto under the Civil Service Act which provides that their tenure of office should be much more permanent than that-have a right to complain if now this house approves of a scheme whereby their positions will be simply at the whim of tire government.
That is as far as dismissals are concerned Now, what about appointments? Supposing that all these men, or a large proportion of them, are dismissed. Under the Civil Service Act when one of these positions became vacant the Civil Service Commission would be requested by the department to advertise for applications, to examine and rate the applicants, and to certify to the minister that such and such a person is entitled to the position. In connection with that there is an express statutory provision that the commission in making the recommendation shall establish a special list on which shall be put the names of those applicants who were on active service, have suffered disability and have not been reestablished. These overseas men thus have a superpreference. It is further required that a list shall be made of applicants who were on active service with His Majesty's land or naval forces or with the forces of the allies, and also that in the same list shall be included the widows of those who died on active service. Those men and women are put on the special list and are entitled to the next preference after the applicants with a disability. What is the effect of these preferences? That if those men get the minimum number of marks required for qualification
they shall have the position in preference to a non ex-soldier who may have very much higher marks. There is another provision that, the age limit which applies to civilian applicants does not apply to ex-servicemen, and that so long as the commission certify the ex-soldier applicant is in physical condition to perform the duties of the office he shall have that office notwithstanding the fact that there is a prescribed age limit.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if these positions were to be filled, and the present law were in force, that would mean ex-servicemen and widows would have that statutory preference, a preference that has been in force since 1919. There have been one or two occasions in this house when attempts have been made to reduce the preference. Only a year ago it was suggested that soldiers of the allies should not be given that preference. I appreciated that the preference was pretty wide in that respect, but I felt it was the entering wedge if any attempt were made to whittle away the preference which the Civil Service Act laid down and I opposed it.
What I have said so far is what would happen if any of these positions were vacant under present conditions where they are under the Civil Service Act. But the committee report proposes to exclude them from that act and to wipe out these advantages, and again to-night I protest against the proposal which is now being made that these preferences and other advantages under the Civil Service Act shall be done away with. I realize quite fully that under order in council 1053, which is referred to in the report of the committee, there is a provision that section 39-which was the old section of the Civil Service Act providing for the ex-soldier preference-shall apply; but having an order in council administered by a government is a very different thing from having an express statutory provision administered by an independent commission. Within the past three or four months I have had the experience of seeing how far one department of this government is prepared to go in disregarding the claims of ex-servicemen. I gave the details of the case the other night, and I will just outline it now. An ex-serviceman who had earned the military cross on the field, had been a resident of the county all his life and had given faithful service in his position, was summarily dismissed without any reason being given or any complaint being made, and a man appointed in his place who had been a resident in the county only five 3'ears and had no overseas service whatever. He was the doctor appointed to look after the Indians in

Civil Service-Report o/ Committee
a portion of my consituency. The expense of appointing the new man to attend the Indians would be double the expense of the ex-service man if he made only one call each year on each person entrusted to his care, the reason being the travelling fees of the new man who was not centrally located. As a matter of fact, we have not yet found out on whose instigation that change was made. The minister rose in his place and announced that he proposed to accept the recommendations of his colleagues or of those in whom he had confidence in making dismissals, even though they concerned ex-service men, without any reasons being given.
Under those circumstances I think I have a right, on behalf of the ex-service men, to look pretty critically on a proposal which places in the hands of the government the jobs of about 3,500 public servants, many of whom are ex-service men who, if this recommendation is accepted, might be dismissed summarily without regard for their preference and have their places filled by civilians, nominees of party friends. The old order in council applied to only a limited class of officials, that is, those in offices where the revenue was $400 or less, as well as certain artisans and labourers expressly mentioned in the order. This provision, however, will apply to about 3,500 office holders all over this dominion, in rural municipalities and villages where the remuneration may be from $200 to $1,300 per year. I submit that, with the pressure I know is exerted on my hem. friends opposite, it will be pretty difficult for them to resist the demands which will be made that they exercise their powers under this proposal.
I say therefore, Mr. Speaker, that because it. gives the government the chance to make summary dismissals and to disregard the returned soldiers' preference altogether, if they so desire, this recommendation should not be adopted. Even leaving out the ex-service men, and on the broader basis that officials should have assurance that they will be continued in office while they give good service, this great body of officials in these positions should not be subject to the will or the whim of any government or any minister, particularly in view of the fact that ever since 1919 we have adopted exactly the opposite principle. While I desire in every way possible to associate myself with the desire for economy, I do look askance at the suggestions now made that it is going to be more economical to appoint these men in the way suggested by thi3 report. As I have said, for the last thirteen years we have had the present provision, under 
which we seem to have done very well, and I have not heard any complaint about t'he expense. Ex-service men have been appointed to these jobs under the statutes of Canada, and it seems to me that this economy, which at most may mean doing away with the sending out of advertisements to those parts of the country where there are vacancies and relieving the staff of the Civil Service Commission of the necessity of looking over these papers and deciding who should be appointed, will amount to very little in comparison with the damage which will be done to the public service. I believe that the adoption of this recommendation will give a very serious setback to the merit system and all that it means in connection wth appointments to the public service.
There are other matters also in respect of which I am very loath to give my support, but I am not going to deal with them. I submit that this is an outstanding example of where the committee, with all due respect, have gone wrong and made a recommendation which this house should not accept. On behalf of the great body of public servants who will be affected, and particularly on behalf of the ex-service men, I protest against this recommendation.
