In rising to say a few words in connection with the report of this committee, of which I had the honour to be a member, I wish first to express to the chairman of the committee my appreciation, of his courtesy and fairness to myself particularly, as the one Labour member on the committee. I do this because the chairman and myself are perhaps quite far apart with regard to politics, economics and social questions and we mignt differ on other occasions in the house, so I wish to express my appreciation now.
In my opinion this is a very good report. As the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Bowman) has pointed out, in order to get a unanimous report of this kind there must be a great deal of give and take between the members of the committee, so it is not strange that when the report comes to the house there should be some parts of it to which hon. members miay object. But I submit that this report, presented by a committee representative of the three distinct groups in the house, is a much better report than could have been brought forward by any one of the three groups. In other words, I think it is a better report than could have been brought in by the four Conservative members of the committee; I think it is a better report than oould have been brought in by the two Liberal members of the committee, and I am almost convinced that it is as good a report as could have been brought in by the Labour member.
The principal objection appears to be to section 25, which excludes from the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission postmasters where the revenue is under $3,000. It might be well to note that at one time all revenue postmasters came under the Civil Service Act, but the Civil Service Commission asked that those receiving under $400 should be excluded from the operations of the act. The recommendation of the committee on this occasion is brought forward largely because of the evidence given by officials of the Post Offjce Department. In my opinion the Post Office Department made these recommendations not because they had any great fault to find with the appointments made by the Civil Service Commission, but because of the delay and expense contingent upon appointments so made. Let me quote from the evidence of Mr. Underwood. From his evidence
I take it that there is no great abjection to the Civil Service Commission making these appointments, but it is felt that in view of the number of dismissals leading to a great many appointments, more expedition is desirable. If something were done to curtail dismissals there would be very little objection to the appointment of postmasters by the commission. Answering a question by myself, he gave the following information. I asked him:
Q. You do not hear so much about the appointment as about the dismissals?-A. There, you put your finger on the sore spot. If you could do something to assist in that matter you would be our everlasting friend.
Further on, I asked him this question:
Q. How are those appointments made now? -A. By the Postmaster General, whichever way he determines.
This refers to post offices under $100. He went on to say:
He may get information from whichever source he deems advisable. He may use the district superintendent, or he may not.
Q. And is that appointment quite satisfactory?-A. Perfectly satisfactory. We have never had any trouble in regard to that. We have less trouble in regard to those than any others. You touched the point this morning when you touched on dismissals. There is where the trouble comes, not in the appointments. We have no trouble with regard to appointments.
Further on, I asked him the following question:
Have you any suggestion to offer as to any improvement in that? Supposing that we assume that the appointment can be made better by the Postmaster General or by the department ?
His answer was:
Just as well, not better, just as well, but more economically.
As regards these appointments, it seems to me that the whole point is this, that they can be made more expeditiously and more economically by the department than by the commission. But in saying that I must add that in my opinion the department is largely to blame for the delays with the commission in making the appointment.
I do not wish to go into every part of the report, and I will only say this, that most of the shortcomings of the present Civil Service Commission are due to the way in which the commissioners themselves are appointed. You cannot have a politically-appointed commission without its being somewhat under the influence of those who appointed it, and if the present government, in appointing the new commission, wishes to have one that will

How that can be accomplished I do not know, but I am sure that if the government desires to have it done it can find a way. As I said before, the report is not perfect, but generally speaking I regard it as a very good report, although looking from this perspective at the amendment offered by the hon. member for Bow River, I will not say that it would not be an improvement on the committee's report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the members
of the civil service committee may I join with the other members of the committee -who have preceded me in expressing my appreciation of the harmonious manner in which its deliberations were conducted.
After listening to the discussion this afternoon it might seem that had it not been for clause 25, the report would have been accepted by the house without comment. My experience teaches me, however, that if clause 25 had not appeared in the report, hon. members would want to pick holes in some other part of it. The report having been unanimous, hon. members must realize that there was a certain amount of compromise amongst members of the committee. As my Liberal colleague has pointed out, undoubtedly had the report been drafted by the two Grits one might have expected a better report. Had we left it entirely to the member from British Columbia I do not think it would have been accepted at all. It was useless, therefore, even to anticipate a report coming either from my friend from Ottawa and myself or from the Labour member. However, we did agree on the report now before the house, and agreed because there was a give and take attitude. In view of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Bow River I think members of the committee should be left free to give expression to their views regarding it. This afternoon I entered the house prepared to give my solid support to the report. If in its wisdom the house sees fit to amend it, I am prepared to submit to its better judgment.
Undoubtedly the outstanding features of the wdiole investigation centred around the personnel of the Civil Service Commission itself. I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier), and I think if hon. members were to scan the evidence submitted before the committee they would find that probably there is only one ground upon which we might arrive at the conclusions that we did regarding the three commissioners. Probably Commissioners Tremblay and MacTavish in the exercise of their duties could be accused-at least the evidence proves to me-only of not exercising the discretionary and statutory powers vested in them. There is no other part of the whole evidence which would suggest to me any reason why the treatment meted out to them should have been suggested.
Apparently, as I have said, the whole objection to the report centres around section 25. I was expecting that the government would be in a position to accept the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Bow River. May I point out to the house, however, that no matter what is contained in the report, whether hon. members decide to do away with the present personnel of the commission or decide to have one, two or three commissioners, the act distinctly states that there shall be no more than three; otherwise the responsibility as to the number is left with the government.
Another feature of the report which has not been discussed is the recommendation that a select special committee of the house be appointed from year to year to make a yearly survey of the operations of the Civil Service Act and the Civil Service Commission. Suppose we allowed clause 25 to go through, and in time it were found that it did not work as some members of the committee and some hon. members of the house believe it will, with the safeguard suggested in the report the condition could be remedied.
After a careful examination of the evidence submitted to the committee I think any person -who views the matter with an unbiased mind will admit that it had grounds on which to make its recommendation-and I am not excepting clause 25. I have been a member of this house since 1925, and as such have sat on many committees. In my experience I have met a good many commissioners, but at no time did I have any personal knowledge of or acquaintance with any of the three civil service commissioners. I met Commissioner Tremblay on one occasion before he became a member of the Civil Service Commission. Therefore I went into that committee unbiased against either the commission or the service. I can assure the house it was an eye-opener to me to sit in on that committee and to investigate the matters which came before us. It gave me an insight into the operation of the Civil Service Act that I do not think I could have acquired in any other way. I am still of opinion that, without the amendment, we could have tried out the recommendation contained in clause 25, because it was based on evidence of those who are unbiased and unprejudiced, officials of the department who are looking just as much as you or I to the efficiency of that department. One thing revealed to our committee was that probably only once in a thousand times was the deputy head of a department not satisfied with an appointment. This proves conclusively that the deputy head of each

department of government is always considered and consulted before an appointment is made. If you go a little further into the evidence you will find that one deputy head, appearing before the committee, pointed out definitely that on more than one occasion, when the eligible list was handed to him, he discarded the whole list and suggested to the commission that they compile another. On one occasion he discovered two eligible lists, and then sought to have the appointment made directly by the commission.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), who has just taken his seat, was good enough to suggest that the government might accept the amendment. Because of that observation I think it is desirable that I should state what I conceive the position to be.

In the month of March a committee of this house, consisting of seven members, was selected to deal with the matters with which we are now all familiar. A unanimous report was made by that committee. I far one feel that the house is to be congratulated upon the fact that seven of its members, professing political allegiance to three, or perhaps four parties, should have been able to arrive at a unanimous conclusion with respect to the matters submitted to them. If this were an ordinary matter in which a jury, having seen the witnesses and heard their testimony, had come back with a unanimous verdict, we would have accepted it without question, assuming there had' been no misapprehension as to what the law was as expressed to them iby the judge who charged them.
In this case I have followed the proceedings only casually; I know what transpired from day to day and I am fairly familiar with the evidence. That unanimous report induced me to believe that the House of Commons was a unit with respect to the matter, and the conclusions at which the committee had arrived were the deliberate conclusions which it was believed the evidence warranted the committee in finding. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat confirms that view, as also did the chairman of the committee (Mr. Lawson), who moved concurrence this afternoon. There is therefore a measure of non-partisanship about the proceedings of the committee. I was much struck by the statement of the hon. member who has just taken his seat that when he went into the committee room he was not even acquainted with some of the members of the commission. The whole approach seems to have been non-partisan. There do not appear to have been those manifestations of party feeling that characterize some committees, and there seems to have been a measure of high regard for established rules, procedure and practice in the conduct of the business of the committee. When I heard the report read, I was pleased, as, I fancy, were other members, to see that in these days of stress and strain seven members of our number had unanimously arrived at conclusions which were rather drastic in some respects. When I heard them I confess I was surprised that with regard to some of them the members of the committee were unanimous.
Under these circumstances, so far as the government are concerned, we assumed that the unanimous judgment of the .committee would be unanimously adapted by the house. Such appears -not to be the case. In view of that fact I rise merely to say it is my earnest wish that those who support the government,

Civil Service-Report oj Committee
will exercise their own personal judgment, regardless of their political affiliations, in voting on this matter. It would be wholly unfair to a committee that has laboured as hard as has this committee, if -the government were to apply, in the words of English parliamentary practice, the whip with respect to the matter. After listening to the speeches that I have heard and to the expressions of tender solicitude for others that so characterized the language of the bon. member for Shelbume-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), I made up my mind that what I have suggested was only fair to those who had given so much time to this question, who have earnestly and, I believe, honestly laboured to bring about a unanimous report, and who, having succeeded in securing that unanimous report and having presented it to the house in that sense, mow because of circumstances over which neither the government nor they have any control, find themselves thrust into a debate which was not expected and which has no doubt embarrassed some of them. I am sure, had I been a member of the committee and been confronted with the situation which has arisen this afternoon, I should likewise have been embarrassed. Therefore I desire to suggest as strongly as I can that each member who sits to the right of the Speaker should exercise his ow.n unfettered and untrammelled judgment in voting either for concurrence im the report or for the amendment now before the house.
Right Hon, W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, like the Prime Minister I felt this afternoon that the house was to be congratulated upon having for the second time this session received from a special committee a unanimous report. I confess that on coming into the house this afternoon I expected the proceedings would be similar to those witnessed yesterday, when the adoption, of the report of another special committee was moved by its chairman, who made a statement which I am sure appealed to all who heard it as broad, tolerant, and devoid of a partisan spirit. He was replied to in a similar vein by an hon. member on this side, who also was a member of the special committee. This afternoon, however, listening to the chairman of the committee whose report we are now considering, I confess that I became more and more surprised as he delved into pages of evidence with a view to extracting here and there what might appear to be a reflection upon some individual who was other than a member of his particular party. I hope I am not going too far when I say that such was the impression pretty generally conveyed, at least to those of us who sit on this side of the house;
and such debate as has arisen has taken place in consequence of that circumstance. It would be amazing if in reviewing a field as wide as that which has been reviewed by the special committee dealing with the administration of the whole civil service there were not found here and there evidences of limitation of discretion, judgment, and the like. I venture to say that if all of us were obliged to review our own acts of the past year there are many things that we should be pleased to eliminate and regard as more or less in the nature of shortcomings. Sometimes we become very critical when we are reviewing the acts of others, and perhaps we are not sufficiently critical in regard to matters that come a little nearer home. Certainly that attitude did affect the temper of the house this afternoon and led, I believe, to the discussion which has taken place.
I believe the report would have been accepted without question had the debate not been provoked in the fashion indicated. I think hon. members generally would have been prepared to allow at least a year to experiment, if I may use that word, with this clause which has provoked so much in the way of discussion, particularly as its operation was being safeguarded, as has been pointed out by members of the committee, by the proposed appointment of a select committee of the house with full power to make hereafter such recommendations as it might think best with respect to the operation of the clause. But now that the debate has taken place it is evident that there are definite reasons for questioning the wisdom of inserting that clause at the moment. I agree with the Prime Minister-I am always happy for a chance to agree with him, and perhaps happier still when he agrees with me, although that is very seldom-that in the circumstances it is only right that notwithstanding the report is unanimous, hon. members should exercise their own individual discretion and judgment in voting upon this amendment.
I have already said in speaking of civil service matters that what I saw of the operation of the Civil Service Act during the time I had to do with the administration of public affairs led me to believe that with regard to many of the minor positions it would be quite as much in the public interest that the member of the house, who is responsible to his own constituency, should have the nomination and the responsibility for appointr ment, with a body such as the Civil Service Commission always determining, before any appointment, that the individual nominated has the necessary qualifications. I thought

there was nothing particularly to be gained, from the point of view of merit, in giving to a body of gentlemen who had no knowledge whatever of the persons they were selecting, the power to choose individuals for positions in the outside service of very small remuneration. The remuneration limit which has been recommended in this case for purposes of exemption goes higher than I would have been prepared to go, but with regard to eliminating a number of the minor positions from the requirement of examinations I have long felt that it was in the public interest that the responsibility should be exercised rather by the member for the constituency than by a group of gentlemen who could not possibly know anything about the qualifications of the individuals, and who could not, in the very nature of things, through an examination, find out who was likely to be the most acceptable person to the community he was to serve. I say that just to indicate the sympathy I have with those who are prepared to support a motion to eliminate a certain number of positions from the operation of the Civil Service Act.
With regard to the broad principle of merit as a basis of entrance into the civil service and of qualification for remaining there, there is no doubt of any kind in my mind; I am wholeheartedly behind the merit system. On account of the limit that has been set in the particular recommendation with regard to postmasters, I shall support the amendment before the house, but I should like every member on this side of the house to feel wholly free to exercise his own judgment with regard to the vote which he may cast.

I should like to say one word on
the motion, because I want clear on the record the contention which I have endeavoured to make and which I am afraid I did not get across to my hon. friend the chairman of the committee. I point out-and I think I am correct-that all these postmasters with whom we are dealing, whom we propose to take from under the Civil Service Act, are under the Civil Service Act at this moment. I point out that the section of the Post Office Act, which gives the Postmaster General the right of removal, makes no distinction between revenue postmasters and any other kind of postmasters, and is no argument whatever in support of the contention that revenue postmasters are to be dealt with on a different basis and are not under the Civil Service Act.
I also pointed out that the Civil Service Act classification, authorized by parliament, contains a classification for revenue postmasters. I doubt very much if the postmasters have thought they were not under the Civil Service Act. They were appointed by the procedure laid down under the act, and they are under the act, according to the classification which was approved by parliament and which is in effect to-day. I think that the act they wanted to be brought under was another act altogether-the Civil Service Superannuation Act. I point out also that the present practice in connection with dismissals from these positions applies both to those who may be dealt with under the Post Office Act and to those who may be dealt with by order in council under the Civil Service Act, and, as I stated a few moments ago, that practice is that there must be an investigation and an adverse finding by a commissioner or a certificate by a member of parliament to the effect that to his personal knowledge there has been partisan work, which I think is the exact wording of the act. I point out also that if these positions are under the Civil Service Act-and there is no doubt about that under the classification-they are entitled to returned soldier preference and that the passing of this resolution takes away from returned soldiers the statutory preference they have hitherto enjoyed with regard to these 3,500 positions throughout this country.

Then they will be in a
better position than postmasters are in at present, until they come under class 2B of the Post Office Department classification. The postmasters referred to in this section are now under the Civil Service Act. Positions from $400 per annum, revenue and up to a salary figure which brings the position automatically under the straight salary system, come under post office classification 2B. Under 2B post offices can be placed under the straight salary only when they reach a certain revenue based upon population, etc.; that is the practice. And when they attain that revenue, based on population, they automatically come under the straight salary system. Once they come under classification 2B they at once become entitled, though they were still under the act before they reached that point, to all the benefits under the Civil Service Pension Act, which is an entirely different statute. The Civil Service Commission therefore fixes the salaries, and for the first year under class 2B the postmaster gets $2,040 a year, his salary being gradually increased year by year, as provided for under the civil service salary classification. No postmaster in the past, in offices with revenue from $400 and upwards, could be appointed to an office if there was a vacancy, unless the commission advertised it. The commission had to advertise it, and not the Post Office department. When the vacancy was advertised and applications were received, they were forwarded to the Civil Service Commission. The commission notified the Post Office Department

that such and such applications had been received and would then request the department to send an inspector or superintendent or other qualified official to interview the applicant and report back to the commission. The report came to the Post Office Department first, was reviewed there and then sent on to the Civil Service Commission. So that every appointment made to a post office with an annual revenue of $400 a year came directly under the Civil Service Act, with the exception that they did not come under it for the purpose of pension and other privileges. Therefore anyone who says that revenue postmasters are not under the act is mistaken. If they are not, why should this committee recommend that they be removed from the operation of the act? Yet that is what is recommended. They recommend that these postmasters be taken from under the operation of the act. They admit themselves, by the report, that such postmasters are under the act, and the reference made by the chairman of the committee to that section of the Post Office Act which gives power to the Postmaster General to remove or to suspend any postmaster or other officer or servant of the post office does not apply in the way the chairman has explained it to the house, because by an order in council which will be found here and which, under the Post Office Act, has equal force with and becomes part of the statute, it is declared how these postmasters, under the Civil Service Act, shall be governed. That order in council was passed in 1922. The Civil Service Act provides that any civil servant who participates in partisan politics shall be dismissed, and the interpretation placed on that was that all postmasters, notwithstanding what the revenue might be, were under the civil service. In 1922 or 1923, however, the Civil Service Commission recommended to the government that postmasters in rural offices with a revenue under $400 a year should be removed from the operation of the act.

I beg the pardon of the house for listening to the interruption of the hon. member. Under the powers given the Civil Service Commission to recommend to the governor in council what positions shall be taken out of or placed under the jurisdiction of the commission, they recommended at the time they sent in their recommendations touching the Post Office Department that a certain number of positions in other departments be taken out. Why did the committee not consider those other departments? They may give the excuse that they could not do so on a revenue basis. Probably not, but it could have been done on a salary basis. Formerly postmasters were put on salaries of $200. On the basis of the revenue they brought in they were placed either beyond or within the control of the civil service commission. In 1926 parliament reduced the postage rate on letters from three to two cents. In view of the reduction in revenue and the hardships caused thereby, an order in council was passed whereby postmasters' commissions were lessened, and their rentals based on revenue lessened. In order to do justice to them the government passed an order in council by which the commission of rural postmasters would be based upon the revenue of the office prior to the introduction of the reduction in postage from three to two cents. That has stood ever since, and it is on that basis that they were paid their commissions until December last when that order in council was rescinded. Now the postmasters are paid simply and only upon the actual revenue received from year to year.

If the committee had gone into other departments and made similar recommendations in regard to them I might see some justification in their action. If I am to believe the report, and if I judge properly from the speeches made this afternoon, I would conclude they have made the change in the Post Office department because they were informed by the chief officials thereof that the work of the department would be lessened. Knowing these officials as I do, I can hardly credit that they would give that as a sufficient reason for placing those men outside the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission, because it must be recognized that their work in the department will be far greater under this recommendation, if it is carried out, than it could have been with those men under the commission. I have faith in the Civil Service Act; I have faith in the merit system, and if in their investigation the committee found anything wrong, why did they not indicate what it was? Why did they not give the real reason that actuated them in making that report? The fact that some of the officials of the Civil Service Commission or of the Post Office Department may have gone astray, may have made mistakes in classification, may have allowed themselves to be influenced by political pull, is no reason why the civil service commissioners should be thrown out of office without the committee giving the public the real reason for which they were put out. remarks made by the former Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot) a little while ago, I would not have considered it necessary to give the house a few of my opinions concerning the report that is now before us. Before I deal with the observations made by the former Postmaster General, may I be permitted to explain the situation that existed in Mundare, a little village in my constituency. In 1926 I came to Ottawa a young man, full of hope, faith and everything else that goes with youth, but I was very much disillusioned after my arrival. A young man, George Woytkiw, approached me in regard to the position of postmaster in Mundare, and for the information of hon. members present may I say that this young man received the largest petition in that district, getting 345 names as against 115 for the other applicant, Mr. Stewart, who was supported by the
defeated candidate. I think possibly the three greatest pests are mosquitos, grasshoppers and, to a member of parliament, defeated candidates-I am adding the latter because nothing gives a member of parliament so much trouble as does a defeated candidate. Mr. Stewart was appointed, there is no doubt in my mind, because of political influence that was exerted in his behalf. The former Postmaster General says that he is in favour of the merit system. As I have already stated, this young man, Woytkiw, received the largest petition; he was also the choice of the district superintendent, and in addition he was very highly recommended over all the other applicants by the chief examiner. In spite of all this merit the Post Office Department recommended the other candidate, namely, the one who received the fewest marks and who was not recommended as first choice by either the district superintendent or the chief examiner or the chairman of the commission.

speechtext:
Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Labour) moved the third reading of Bill No. 72, respecting relief measures.
2882	COMMONS
Unemployment-Agreements with Provinces

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES RESPECTING MEASURES TO RELIEVE DISTRESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
as I mentioned on the second reading, this is the fourth measure which the present administration has introduced with respect to unemployment relief. The house having heard so frequently and emphatically the views of the official opposition on the features of the previous bills, which gave to the administration a blank cheque and also the power to legislate by order in council with respect to matters which in our opinion should be reserved to the House of Commons and the Senate, it would hardly be expected that we would acquiesce in this particular measure and readily give to it our support. However, those who were in the house yesterday must have been impressed with the statement made by the Minister of Labour that it was then the eleventh of the month, and that since the first day of May there had not been in existence any legislation -which would permit of the government entering into any agreements with the provinces in regard to this all-important matter of unemployment relief, and that that power would not be possessed by the administration until the legislation here proposed had passed this house and the Senate and had received royal assent. Other hon. members made reference to the extent to which there is actual suffering in the country at the moment on the part of large numbers through the absence of the means to satisfy their wants. Were the circumstances other than as described, certainly we of the opposition would move in amendment to this motion for the third reading, to refer the bill back to the committee of the whole house to reconsider certain of its aspects.
What we particularly deplore about the measure is the absence of evidence of any policy on the part of the government with respect to unemployment relief. Up to the present time there has been at least a profession on the part of the administration that it would endeavour to carry out its promises to provide work-not only to provide work, but to end unemployment through work that would be provided. But so far as this bill is concerned, having regard to what has been stated by the minister himself and to the provisions of the bill, it is perfectly clear that the government has thrown overboard completely whatever intention in the way of policy it may have had to provide work as a means of ending unemployment. The present measure substitutes, so far as the federal government is concerned, contributions to the provinces for the purpose of administering doles where such may be necessary to meet the demand of immediate relief.

Coming at the end of almost two years of office and being all that the administration can offer, especially after its members have had a free hand and the experience which comes with office in dealing with important questions, it is a lamentable confession of complete failure to cope with this all-important question and to offer to the country anything in the nature of a constructive policy. However, I suppose for those who are suffering, anything in the shape of assistance is better than nothing, and for that reason, having regard also to the lateness of the session, we do not propose in any way to delay the giving of such relief as the government may still intend to give through the provinces in accordance with what apparently is their only method, namely the method provided here. While, for the reasons mentioned, we are prepared to allow the bill to pass third reading without amendment, we desire, at the same time, to register as strongly as we can our protest against the measure in the form in which it is, renewing as it does the objectionable feature of the blank cheque, which deprives this House of Commons of the control which it should have over expenditures and consequent taxation, and the equally, if not more, objectionable feature of giving to the governor in council power to legislate, notwithstanding the existence of any law or statute, with respect to matters which we believe should be legislated upon only by the Commons and the Senate. With this protest, Mr. Speaker, and at the same time with the hope that by expediting the enactment to the extent which may thus be possible, we shall be serving a helpful end, we do not at this time propose to offer further opposition.
I have just this one further word to add. It is most regrettable that this measure, which deals with the most important subject which has come up this session, should have been left for the purposes of discussion, as has been the case with similar measures in previous years, until the closing weeks of the session. I said at the time the Unemployment Relief Continuance Act was introduced that the government should at that time, instead of introducing a temporary measure, have then brought down its legislation with respect to relief measures in order that there might be ample time for discussion. The fact that as matters now stand we are half a month beyond the period during which any relief for the new fiscal year can be given under legislation relative thereto is something for which the government itself is wholly responsible.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference

The house in committee of supply, Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
To provide for expenses in connection with the Imperial economic conference, $250,000.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I may say there will be
an additional item in the supplementary estimates, so that another opportunity will be afforded for discussion.

Mr. Chairman, as I intimated the other day, I am particularly anxious to offer a few suggestions to the Prime Minister -if I may put it that way-as the Imperial economic conference is perhaps of greater interest and importance to the people of the part of Nova Scotia from which I come than any other matter that has came before the house this session. While what I shall put forward will be general in its nature and national in its application, I may, perhaps take as a starting point the interests of the apple growers and apple exporters of Nova Scotia..
The apple exporting industry of Canada is in many respects a typical exporting industry, depending to a very large extent upon the market of the United Kingdom. I have the figures here, but I will not weary the committee with details; I propose to state the main features of the situation. The dominion exports about one third of its total apple production to the United Kingdom market. During the last five years our production has averaged about 3,500,000 barrels, of which from 1,100,000 to 1,200,000 barrels have found a market in Great Britain.
Our competitors in the United Kingdom market are the British themselves, who raise quite a large quantity of fruit, and more particularly the apple growers of the United States. The situation in the United States differs from the situation in Canada in this respect, that they have an enormous production in that country. It is very difficult to get figures showing the exact production, but it is from 125,000,000 to 250,000,000 bushels per annum. This production is largely marketed in the United States.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, but I cannot hear the hon. gentleman.

I was saying, Mr. Chairman, that while we in Canada export about one-third of our total production of apples to the United Kingdom-and the greater part of our exports go to the United Kingdom-the same is not true of the United States, our chief competitor in that market. They export twice as large a quantity of apples to the United
Kingdom as we do, but that is an insignificant proportion of their total production. I should like to make this feature of the apple exporting situation perfectly clear; while their production is huge, it varies greatly. The surplus they export varies greatly also, but that surplus is only a very small proportion of their total production, amounting to not more than seven per cent or eight per cent at the most. The result is that in a year of heavy production in the United States at times we find the British market almost ruined by these large American surpluses.
For these reasons it is important that the present preference, with which I shall deal in a moment, should be preserved if possible. The tariff preference in the British market at present, under the Import Duties Act which came into effect on March 1, 1932, is ten per cent. Before I go into that, in order to put the matter clearly perhaps I should read a summary of an extract from the report of the Imperial economic committee of 1926. Your attention is called specifically to the following points:
(1)	That in the United States there is the
home market offered by the population of 115,000.000 consuming more fruit per head than the population of the United Kingdom. The exported surplus averages some 7 per cent of the total crop.	.
(2)	That Canada on the other hand, with a population of only 9,000,000 must export at least 30 per cent of the total crop or more than four times as high a proportion as the United States. The export trade is vital to the Canadian apple grower and merely incidental to the American grower.
(3)	That the American apple market is protected by a customs tariff and that it has been particular to avoid glutted market conditions on the home market by throwing the bolk of the increase into the export trade. The arrival of these dumped surpluses and indeed the mere knowledge that they would be forthcoming from the other side of the Atlantic tends to wreck the markets. The effect is to wreck the prospects of the home and Canadian growers.
Along the same line I should like to quote from a book called Imperial Economic Unity, written by the late Sir Alfred Mond, Lord Melchett. At page 149 he says:
Both Australian and Canadian official reports state that in recent years the apple industry has declined and the acreage under cultivation has become slightly less, owing to difficulties experienced in disposing of their production. The principal contributory factor to this is the varying surplus production of the United States of America.
At page 150 he states:
The export trade of the American fruit grower is merely a matter of the disposal of surplus production, whereas in Canada and Australia a steady and assured export market is vital to the very existence of the industry.

The Canadian Horticultural Council has been studying the problem, and the figures they give to the public indicate that the United Kingdom imports about 5,000,000 barrels of apples each year and that at present Canada is supplying not nearly half those requirements, but that there is capacity for development of production in Canada and in Australasia to the extent necessary to take care of the entire import requirements of the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Is it not also true that you must have regard to climatic conditions and seasonal demands in order that other countries may also serve those seasonal demands having regard to the climatic conditions under which apples are produced?
I speak subject to correction, but my answer would be that between Canada, Australasia and South Africa the entire import requirements of the United Kingdom could be met.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is right.
The United States does not serve a complementary purpose at all, their apples go in during the same season that apples are imported from Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is exactly what I endeavoured to show, that other portions of the empire in addition to Canada are producing apples that could supply the English market at other seasons.

That is right. I think the material factors in the situation are, first, a large and immensely valuable market for apples in the United Kingdom; second, the capacity of the British dominions to acquire and supply a large part of that market; third, the menace of the competition of huge and varying surpluses of United States apples in that market; fourth, the special importance of that market to the province of Nova Scotia, which is particularly adapted to the export of apples to Great Britain and from which come the great bulk of apples exported from Canada; fifth, the value of a preference on apples in that market, and sixth, the great and paramount importance of free entry into that market.
That brings me, Mr. Chairman, to some general considerations with regard' to the preferences that now exist. I may say that preferences in Great Britain have been built up over a long period of years. I do not want to go too far back into history, but of course there were the preferences under the Navigation Acts, which ceased when the Navigation

Acts were repealed in 1847, when free trade came in. Those preferences were not suited to present conditions, although the Canadian lumber trade between 1807 and 1847 was built up on 'the colonial preferences which existed for about two centuries before the advent of free trade in 1846. Between 1847 and 1897 there were no preferences between Great Britain and the dominion, but in 1897 Canada introduced a voluntary British preference. This country was followed by the other British dominions; in 1903 New Zealand extended voluntary preferences to Great Britain. In 1904 South Africa followed, in 1907 Australia followed, and then a great many other parts of the British Empire followed with these voluntary preferences. Perhaps the membere of the committee will be surprised to know the ramifications of the voluntary preferential system throughout the British Empire. These are some of the parts of the empire which extend preferences to Great Britain: the Irish Free State, whose preference came into effect in 1923; Northern Rhodesia; Southern Rhodesia; India, which gives a small preference on certain classes of iron and steel goods; Fiji; the Bahamas; Jamaica; St. Lucia; St. Vincent; Barbados; the Virgin Islands; Grenada; St. Christopher; Nevis; Antigua; Montserrat; Trinidad; Tobago; Dominica; British Honduras; British Guiana; Cyprus; Mauritius; Brunei; Gibraltar; British North Borneo; Bermuda; and Samoa. That widespread and farreaching system of voluntary preferences has grown up, not upon the basis of bargaining of quid pro quo at all; they are voluntary preferences. The first protective element introduced by Great Britain into her fiscal system after the abolition of protection, between 1846 and 1860, was introduced in 1915 with the McKenna duties. The only duties before that, in all that interval-that is, anything that could be called protective- were the wheat duties between 1902 and 1903, which were very small and soon repealed, and the tobacco duty in 1904.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A shilling a quarter.

The tobacco duties were
reduced a year or two afterwards. In 1915, however, as a war measure, the McKenna duties came into effect. Those duties applied to musical instruments, clocks and watches, and cinematograph films, if I remember rightly. They were introduced, as I say, more as a war measure than a trade measure, first, to save space in ships taking raw materials to Britain, and secondly, to relieve the exchange situation as between Great Britain and the United States. No preferences were provided when the McKenna duties were first imposed,

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
but in 1919 preferences were granted to the dominions and colonies by the Finance Act of that year, and then followed a rapid and very notable extension of preferential treatment to the dominions and colonies. As I have said, the preferences began in 1919. In 1920 the Importation of Dyestuffs Act provided for the prohibition of the importation of dyestuffs into Britain, but not from parts of the British Empire. In 1921 the Safeguarding of Industries Act was introduced, providing for the imposition of duties on key industry goods and on other goods after inquiry, but under that act no duties were imposed against British Empire goods. In 1923 the Irish Free State, which had come into existence, obtained the benefit of the preferences that were given to the other parts of the empire, and in that year also was held the Imperial economic conference to which my right hon. leader referred the other day, and preferences were arranged for at that conference on a large number of articles. Mr. Baldwin was, I think, Prime Minister of Great Britain at that time; at any rate, the Conservative party was in power there. Before these duties could be brought into effect Mr. Baldwin went to the people on a platform of protection and was defeated, and consequently when the new parliament met in 1924 its membership was opposed to protection and therefore the preferences arranged for at the Imperial economic conference of 1923 did not come into effect. I may mention, in reference to apples, that it was agreed at the conference of 1923 that there should be a preference on raw apples. It was proposed to levy a duty of five shillings a hundredweight on raw apples of foreign origin, and to continue to admit raw apples from the empire free of duty. Then in 1925, 1926, 1927 and 1928 there were extensions every year of preferences to the dominions and other parts of the British Empire as new duties were imposed; and then, of course, this year, cairue the Import Duties Act which placed a duty of ten per cent upon nearly all goods entering the United Kingdom, the chief exceptions being wheat, in grain, meat, including bacon, raw cotton, raw wool, fish of British catch, newspapers and newsprint in rolls containing not less than -seventy per cent mechanical wood pulp, wood pulp itself, raw rubber, iron ore, tin ore and shipbuilding materials consigned direct to shipbuilding yards. The extent of these preferences that have gradually been granted by the United Kingdom to the dominions is shown by a book I have in my hand, and to which I have referred, by Lord Melchett, in which he gives the percentages of imported
dutiable goods upon which preference is given. These goods, from empire countries, are: tea, 84-8 per cent; cocoa, raw, 93-4 per cent; coffee, 50-9 per cent; sugar, raw and refined, 38 per cent; raisins, 27-7 per cent; motor cars, 20-9 per cent, and many others. This shows that quite a large proportion of the imports in important lines that went into the United Kingdom came from the British dominions and colonies under preferential tariffs.
The Import Duties Act provides that these preferences shall lapse on the 15th day of November as against the dominions but not as against the colonies. That, I think, is a significant fact. It is only against the dominions which have imposed, practically all of them, protective tariffs, and in some cases very high protective tariffs against the mother country; it is only as against these that the preferences shall lapse on November 15. It is of great importance to the part of Canada from which I come, and needless to say it is of great importance to Canada as a whole, that this government, at the forthcoming Imperial economic conference, should so conduct negotiations that there be an extension of these preferences past the 15th day of November.
The conclusions which I would draw from the facts I have put forward are, first, that without the introduction of bargaining at all as between the units of the empire, there has come into existence a gradually evolving system of preferences, which would probably have accomplished all and perhaps more than all that the Imperial economic conference will accomplish; secondly, that had it not been for the hostile tariffs of the dominions, imposed by legislation or by orders in council, the preferences under the Import Duties Act would probably have been unlimited as to duration, as they were in the case of the colonies, instead of being limited to a period expiring on November 15 next.

Yes, but the point is this.
My right hon. friend, at the Imperial conference of 1930, indicated that it was desirable, in his opinion, that we simply give preference for preference, that we grant pref-

erences upon a bargaining basis. He took the view that this was the only businesslike way in which to do it. Great Britain has on every occasion on which she had imposed protective duties extended substantial preferences to the dominions. But very sensibly she took the view that if trade was to be upon a bargaining basis she would give the dominions bargaining. That is to say she would make her preferences lapse on November 15 so that she would have something to bargain with. That policy would never have been adopted had it not been for the interjection by the Prime Minister at the Imperial economic conference in 1930 of that new element in trade relations between the different parts of the British Empire.
In my constituency we knew that just as soon as Great Britain got to the place where she deemed it advisable in her interests to impose protective tariffs on apples we would go in on a preferred basis, and retain freedom of entrance into that market. However, the introduction by our Prime Minister of this new principle at the Imperial economic conference of 1930 upset the development of the whole system, so that when they brought in their duties on March 1, 1932, they put a time limit on, and now we are faced with the necessity of negotiation as to whether our apples and other goods will continue to enter that market free.
I should say it is of far more importance that we continue to get into the market than that we receive a preference, but with duties that debar us. Freedom of entrance may be more important than protection in the market. Freedom of entrance into that market on preferential terms would have come with the coming into effect of a protective system in Great Britain without bargaining at all, in the natural course of events as indicated by the facts I have given to the committee.
My submission is that the present government's policy in Imperial trade relations has been unfortunate, and that if we are to continue the progress that has been made a reversal of that policy is essential. Now, what are the principles that should guide the government at the conference? It seems to me at the forthcoming Imperial economic conference we should not, if we can help it, tie our hands so far as negotiations with foreign countries are concerned. We may depend upon it that the United Kingdom will not tie its hands in those relations. Great Britain has close trade relations with the Argentine republic, the Scandinavian countries and other countries which treat them better in their markets than we treat them in ours.

Not long ago Mr. Runciman made a speech in which he said:
We are bound and determined to make arrangements for our own dominions during this summer and autumn which will add to our volume of trade between us and them, but that does not preclude us from making friendly arrangements with foreign countries, friendly arrangements to which I look forward with great hope.
You can be sure we are sufficiently open-minded to prevent any policies standing in the way of the development of world trade.
The Dominion of Canada also is so constituted that it can deal advantageously with countries outside the British Empire. During recent years there has grown up what might be termed a state of tariff war between Canada and the United States. I do not think, however, many of us believe that condition will continue indefinitely. These two countries are so situated that a very large and profitable trade must be done between them. I submit it would be unwise at the Imperial conference for Canada so to tie her hands that she could not negotiate with countries such as the United States, a country with which she can do business under such peculiarly favourable conditions.
The same is true of Germany. Since I have sat in this house I have had representations year after year from people in my constituency asking that I do something or get the government to do something to improve trade relations with Germany. There we have very hostile tariffs against us. In some cases their tariffs against us are twice as high as they are against the United States. If it could be avoided it would be unwise for the Dominion of Canada at the coming conference to tie its hands as to negotiations with countries with which she can trade profitably. It must be remembered that the trend during the last twenty years has been in the direction of a greater percentage of trade with foreign countries. I have before me figures for the years 1911 and 1932. In 1911, 54.3 per cent of our exports were to other parts of the British Empire; in 1932, the figure was only 38 per cent. In 1911, 28.7 per cent of our imports were from other parts of the British Empire, whereas in 1932, the figure was only 25.5 per cent. In that connection there is a substantial reduction in both cases, but especially as to the percentage of exports. As to the United States, the percentage of our total trade has remained about the same. In 1911, 38 per cent of our exports were to the United States, and in 1932 there was an increased figure of 40.8 per cent. In 1911, 60.8 per cent of our imports were from the United

Supply-Imperial Economic Conference
States, and in 1932, the figure was exactly the same. In other words our trade with our neighbouring country, in percentage of total trade during the last twenty-one years has remained practically the same. When we come to other foreign countries, however, we see during that period a great increase in the percentage of trade. In 1911, 7.7 per cent of our exports were to other foreign countries; in 1932 the figure was 21.2 per cent. In 1911, 10.5 per cent of our imports were from other foreign countries, whereas in 1932 there has been an increase to 13.7 per cent. That is to say, the percentage of our exports to other foreign countries, countries other than the United States and parts of the British Empire, during the past twenty-one years has been multiplied by three. We would be unwise to fly in the face of that trend, especially when it it considered that in all probability a great many foreign countries will be negotiating with one another and with us for the reduction of tariffs during the next few years.
Another guiding principle that should prevail at the Imperial economic conference is that we should attempt to increase and expand, not merely deflect trade. I believe that is the most fundamental and the soundest criticism of the enormous duties which during the last year and a 'half we have placed against British products. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth placed on Hansard during his speech on the budget some rates to which I should like to make reference. When dumping duties and tariff rates were added together some of them went as high as 99 per cent ad valorem. Some of the rates were 94 per cent, 43 per cent, 99 per cent, 75 per cent, 46} per cent, 41 per cent, and so on. The erection of these very high tariffs against Great Britain has reduced the volume of trade. If the effects of such tariffs were merely to deflect trade, if it meant merely that buyers bought from Canadian instead of British sources, it would not be so unfortunate, but it means that not only do they change their sources of supply but they do not buy as much. The total volume of trade is cut down. If there is one thing upon which leading economists in the world of to-day agree-and I refer to men such as John Maynard Keynes

it is the importance of getting people to buy and sell in a larger way. If the world is to recover from the depression there must be an expansion of the volume of trade. Consequently any development at the Imperial economic conference which simply deflects without increasing trade will not be in the best interests either of this country or of the
world as a whole. A policy which means merely that the empire will erect around its borders a high tariff, leaving the high tariffs still existing between the various parts of the empire, will reduce rather than increase the total volume of trade and will not be in the best interests of Canada. I urge that consideration with the greatest confidence and earnestness upon the Prime Minister. The idea put forward at the Imperial conference of 1930 that every industry we can get going in this country we must protect by high tariffs against the other parts of the empire and then put around the empire itself another high tariff against the rest of the world, is not in line with what economists or, for that matter, business men or statesmen, are now urging. The advice that is being given in increasing volume is to adopt policies that will stimulate and increase the total volume of trade.
Finally I would say this: We should avoid the establishment of an Imperial economic unit or zollverein which will isolate us from the rest of the world and provoke other nations to form themselves into similar exclusive trading confederacies. I do not think it is necessary to elaborate that thought. Anyone who has been reading the articles in the magazines and the speeches that are being made will see the great danger of making of the British Empire a zollverein such as the German states constituted in the last century. In the Round Table of March, 1932, there was a very thoughtful article on Imperial preference, and the conclusion to which the writer of that article came, I adopt, because it seems to me very sensible. It reads:
Let us now sum up what seem to he the fundamentals of any system of Imperial trade regulation, including preference, which is to be of lasting value. It must take into account the fundamental economic policies of the participants, including the balance between their industry and agriculture, and their commercial relations with the rest of the -world. Once those essentials have been determined, it should imply a progress towards a lowering of tariffs and the breakdown of economic nationalism generally; it must expand rather than diminish the volume of world trade. While for the time being it may injure third parties it must not be directed against them, and must leave them an opportunity of participating in preferential advantages in exchange of equivalent undertakings. It must not be of such complication or duration as to tie the hands of any party unduly in its trading relations either within or outside the commonwealth. Above all, it must be based on the principle of mutual advantage and free consent.
It is fashionable at present to say that we should make suggestions as to what we should give at this conference rather than what we should seek to get. I can think of many
